title: API keys versus tokens
summary: When a long-lived API key is fine, when you need tokens, and how to issue, store and check keys properly.

steps.title: Two kinds of credential
body: **API keys** are long random strings given to a *client application*, sent on every request (`X-Api-Key: dk_live_...` or `Authorization: ApiKey ...`).
**Access tokens** (usually JWTs from OAuth) are short-lived, issued by an authorization server, and can represent a **user** and a **delegated scope**.
| Identifies | an application / account | a user *and* an app, or a service |
| If leaked | works until someone notices and revokes it | works until `exp` |
| Revocation | delete the key (one lookup per request) | wait for `exp`, or extra machinery |
| Good for | server-to-server integrations, developer APIs (Stripe, SendGrid), metering | anything acting for a user; zero-trust service meshes |

An API key **must never be embedded in a browser or mobile app**: anything shipped to a device is public. A key in front-end code identifies a *project* at best (as with map tile APIs), never authenticates anyone.

steps.prompt: API key or user access token?
items: A partner's nightly server job pushing orders
Metering a paying developer's usage of your SMS API
A mobile app reading the signed-in user's messages
A single-page app updating the user's profile
A third-party app acting for one of your users

steps.title: Issuing and checking keys properly
body: - **Generate** 32 random bytes and add a readable **prefix**: `dk_live_` + 43 base64url characters. The prefix tells you (and secret scanners on GitHub) what the string is, and a `test` vs `live` prefix stops test keys hitting production.
- **Show it once.** Store only a **hash**. Like refresh tokens, keys are long random values, so SHA-256 is enough; a slow password hash would make every request slow.
- **Look up by hash.** Hash the incoming key and look up the hash. A dictionary lookup on a hash doesn't leak the secret through timing, because an attacker can't steer the hash byte by byte.
- **Scope** every key (`reports:read`), give it an owner and an expiry, and make rotation easy: allow two active keys per client so they can swap without downtime.
- **Rate-limit** per key, and log the key's *id* or prefix, never the key.

steps.explain: The database never holds the key itself, so a leaked table of hashes doesn't hand out working keys.

steps.prompt: Generate a prefixed API key and the value to store.
A developer pastes a live API key into a public GitHub repository. Which design choice limits the damage most?
options: A recognisable prefix, so GitHub's secret scanning flags it and you can revoke it within minutes
Making the key 16 characters instead of 64
Storing the key in plain text so support staff can read it back

steps.prompt: Why is SHA-256 acceptable for storing API keys when it is far too fast for passwords?
options: API keys are 256 random bits, so there is no dictionary to guess from; passwords are human-chosen and guessable
It isn't acceptable; API keys need Argon2

steps.title: API key middleware with scopes
prompt: The starter stores two keys **as SHA-256 hashes** with their scopes. **Run checks** starts the server and calls it.
- Middleware: every path except `/health` needs an `X-Api-Key` header whose SHA-256 hex is in `apiKeys`; otherwise `401 {"error": ...}`. Put the `ApiClient` in `ctx.Items["client"]`.
- `GET /reports` needs scope `reports:read`, `POST /reports` needs `reports:write`; a known key without the scope gets `403`.
starter: // Only hashes are stored. The keys themselves were shown to their owners once, at creation.
solution: // Only hashes are stored. The keys themselves were shown to their owners once, at creation.
await ctx.Response.WriteAsJsonAsync(new { error = "A valid X-Api-Key header is required." });
app.MapPost("/reports", (HttpContext ctx) => Need(ctx, "reports:write") ?? Results.Created("/reports/q3", new { id = "q3" }));
hints: A helper `IResult? Need(HttpContext ctx, string scope)` returning `null` when allowed lets you write `Need(ctx, "reports:read") ?? Results.Ok(...)`.
template: public static async Task Run(HttpClient http)
await Dojo.TryAsync("API keys could be checked", async () =>
Dojo.Eq("GET /health needs no key", "ok", await DojoWeb.Text(await Send(http, HttpMethod.Get, "/health", null)));
DojoWeb.Status("GET /reports without a key gets 401", 401, await Send(http, HttpMethod.Get, "/reports", null));
DojoWeb.Status("a wrong key gets 401", 401, await Send(http, HttpMethod.Get, "/reports", "dk_reports_0000"));

DojoWeb.Status("the stored hash itself is not a key", 401, await Send(http, HttpMethod.Get, "/reports", Convert.ToHexString(System.Security.Cryptography.SHA256.HashData(System.Text.Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes(Reader)))));
DojoWeb.Status("the reader key can GET /reports", 200, await Send(http, HttpMethod.Get, "/reports", Reader));
DojoWeb.Status("the reader key can't POST /reports (403)", 403, await Send(http, HttpMethod.Post, "/reports", Reader));
DojoWeb.Status("the ingest key can POST /reports", 201, await Send(http, HttpMethod.Post, "/reports", Writer));
DojoWeb.Status("a key for /health doesn't hurt", 200, await Send(http, HttpMethod.Get, "/health", "garbage"));
static Task<HttpResponseMessage> Send(HttpClient http, HttpMethod m, string url, string? key)
if (key is not null) msg.Headers.Add("X-Api-Key", key);
